key_concepts.summary: Boxing rewards legal, effective punching and round control, not just activity volume.
Ring geography matters: center ring, ropes, corners, exits, pivots, pressure lanes, and escape routes should be modeled.
Boxing is structured as repeated rounds separated by short rest; training should respect round-rest rhythm.
Olympic boxing and professional boxing differ in bout length, judging context, equipment, and competition demands.
Boxing is weight-class based; training must not ignore body mass, nutrition, recovery, and weigh-in timing.
A boxer ahead on rounds, down on rounds, hurt, fatigued, or facing a southpaw requires different tactical decisions.

technical_models.backend_use: Tag drills by ring zone and range.

tactical_rules.rule: Use center-ring work to teach initiative, range control, and escape options before advanced pressure/corner tactics.
Rope work can be defensive or tactical, but beginners should not be trapped there without exit skills.
Early round work should include reading stance, lead hand, distance, speed, and opponent rhythm.
Late-round tactics should bias simple high-percentage actions when fatigue reduces fine motor control.
Do not generate dehydration or rapid weight-loss prescriptions; refer severe weight-making issues to qualified professionals.

physical_demands.quality: aerobic recovery between bursts and rounds
calf, ankle, hip, and trunk endurance
head-position control and force transfer support

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Contact exposure carries concussion and cumulative head-impact risk.
Punching volume, poor wrapping, and impact quality can overload hand and wrist structures.
High punching volume can overload shoulder and scapular control.
Fatigued neck and poor defensive posture can increase vulnerability.
Aggressive body-mass manipulation can harm performance and health.

training_implications.summary: Conditioning should often use round lengths, rest intervals, and tactical tasks.
New technical skills should be learned before fatigue-based conditioning.
Fight-camp, taper, and post-fight weeks should be different from general training.
Sparring and contact volume must be tracked separately from gym workload.
Nutrition logic should support performance and safety, not extreme cutting.
